title: Is there a disease that kills by preventing sleep?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore fatal familial insomnia (FFI), a rare, inherited prion disease that destroys the thalamus and sleep-regulating parts of the hypothalamus, causing progressive insomnia and death typically within one to three years. They explain prion diseases as misfolded proteins that can infect other proteins, trace the suspected 1765 and 1836 Venice cases, go through the four clinical stages, discuss diagnosis, palliative treatment with GHB, and gene therapy hopes. They also cover kuru, sporadic and acquired routes, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (including the French growth hormone outbreak), mad cow disease, chronic wasting disease, Stanley Prusiner's work, and the 2005 University of Texas experiment. The episode closes with a listener mail about a farm accident and Robert Pickton.

segments.title: Opening banter and Jerry's sleepless night
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about a sleepless night and the nature of insomnia, then introduce fatal familial insomnia as a rare, familial, fatal disease.

segments.title: Origins of fatal familial insomnia and prion diseases
segments.summary: The hosts describe FFI's rarity, its inherited pattern, and the suspected Venice cases from 1765 and 1836. They introduce prion diseases as a group of spongiform, neurodegenerative conditions and note the absence of an inflammatory response.

segments.title: Prions as misfolded proteins and how they infect
segments.summary: Explanation that prions are misfolded proteins with no DNA or RNA, the normal PrP^C versus misfolded PrP^Sc, the gene polymorphism behind the abnormal protein, and how misfolded proteins convert normal ones. Mention of Stanley Prusiner and the 2005 University of Texas work.

segments.title: Three routes of infection: acquired, sporadic, inherited
segments.summary: The hosts describe the three ways prion disease arises. Kuru in Papua New Guinea is the acquired example, linked to funerary cannibalism. Sporadic cases arise without known cause, and FFI is mostly inherited. They speculate about the Venice cases.

segments.title: Symptoms and four stages of fatal familial insomnia
segments.summary: Symptoms common to prion diseases are listed, followed by FFI's hallmark insomnia and the four stages: progressive insomnia with anxiety and panic, sympathetic hyperactivity, near-total sleeplessness, and end-stage akinetic mutism leading to coma and death. Typical onset is around age fifty and survival is one to three years.

segments.title: Brain mechanism: thalamus and sleep regulation
segments.summary: Prions damage the thalamus and hypothalamus, especially the anti-waking neurons that normally keep the brain asleep. Glial cells form scar tissue (gliosis), so the brain can no longer transition into deep sleep, and the insomnia accelerates decline.

segments.title: Diagnosis, treatment, and gene therapy
segments.summary: Diagnosis is hard and relies on patient history plus tests such as MRI, PET scan, EEG and spinal tap. There is no cure, only palliative care, including GHB given for short bouts of sleep. Gene therapy is discussed as a possible future cure.

segments.title: Other prion diseases: CJD, mad cow, chronic wasting disease, scrapie
segments.summary: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is introduced, with its sporadic, inherited and acquired forms, and its link to mad cow disease. Chronic wasting disease in deer and elk and scrapie in sheep and goats are mentioned. The French growth hormone outbreak from pituitary glands is described.

segments.title: Prion skepticism and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts recount skepticism toward prions, including Alzheimer's comparisons and scrapie strain arguments, and the 2005 test-tube experiment. They end with a joke about the danger of prion disease to humanity.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and show contact information.
